passage:
Every Sunday at four, my grandfather Omkar tells me about the day the river flooded his village. I'm Deepak, and I've heard it maybe thirty times: the boat, the tin trunk, his mother carrying the brass lamp. When I was fifteen I would say, "Nana, I know." Now I just settle into the chair and ask something new.
Last week I asked, "What did the water smell like?" He stopped, looked at the ceiling, and said, "Like wet earth and burnt wood." He had never said that before. His eyes went shiny. I think he wants the story remembered more than he wants me to learn from it.

qa.q: What does Omkar tell Deepak about every Sunday at four?
qa.a: Omkar tells Deepak about the day the river flooded his village.

qa.q: What does Omkar's shiny-eyed reaction suggest Omkar was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests Omkar felt moved and glad to be asked something new. Recalling a smell no one had asked about brought the memory closer.

qa.q: What does Deepak do each time the story is told again, and what does it lead to?
qa.a: Deepak settles in and asks a new question each time. Asking what the water smelled like drew out a detail Omkar had never told before.

qa.q: How might Omkar have felt when Deepak said "Nana, I know" at fifteen?
qa.a: Omkar might have felt a little dismissed, as if the story mattered less to the listener than to the teller. Now the new question shows the story is being kept.

grounding: A young adult lets an elder tell the same story again, asking a new question each time, since elders often want to be heard and remembered.

passage:
I watch from my balcony, since Yamini's family sits in the courtyard below every evening. Yamini's Nani was on the cot, telling the flood story again. I've heard it drift up at least four times. She always starts: "That year the river came at midnight."
Yamini, elbows on knees, listened as if it were new. Then Yamini asked, "Nani, who carried the little ones?" The old woman lit up, her hands started moving, and she named two names I'd not heard before.
Yamini didn't correct or hurry her. When it was done Nani patted Yamini's cheek. I don't know what Yamini thinks each time, but Yamini never looks bored.
— Zainab, neighbour

qa.q: Where does Yamini sit while Nani tells the flood story?
qa.a: Yamini sits in the courtyard, with elbows on knees, near the cot.

qa.q: What might Nani have felt when Yamini asked "who carried the little ones?"
qa.a: Nani seems to have felt delighted and eager, since Nani lit up and started moving hands. Zainab can only judge from what shows outwardly.

qa.q: What does Yamini do each time the story is repeated?
qa.a: Yamini listens as if it were new, asks a fresh question and does not correct or hurry Nani. That draws out details that Nani names.

qa.q: What does Zainab see in Yamini's way of listening?
qa.a: Zainab sees patient interest, since Yamini never looks bored. Zainab does not claim to know Yamini's thoughts, only what the listening looks like.

grounding: A young adult lets an elder tell the same story again and asks a new question, observed by a neighbour.

passage:
Friday. Dadu started the story of the 1988 flood again at dinner. Bhupen's cousin Sahil rolled his eyes; they'd heard it maybe forty times. Bhupen put down his phone. "Dadu, what did the water smell like?"
Dadu stopped, surprised. "Like mud and diesel. And fear."
Tuesday. The flood story came again. This time Bhupen asked, "Who rowed the boat?"
"A fisherman called Pobitro. He never took a single rupee." Dadu's voice went soft. "I never thanked him properly."
The next Sunday, Dadu told it once more. Sahil stayed at the table this time and asked, "Did you ever find Pobitro again?"
Dadu looked at both of them for a long moment. "No. But you two know his name now."
Afterward, Bhupen wrote the name, Pobitro, and the smell of mud and diesel in a notebook he'd started keeping.

qa.q: What did Dadu say the flood water smelled like?
qa.a: Dadu said it smelled like mud and diesel, and fear.

qa.q: What was Dadu feeling when he spoke about Pobitro?
qa.a: Dadu felt tender and regretful, his voice going soft because he never thanked Pobitro properly.

qa.q: What did Bhupen do that changed how the story felt?
qa.a: He put down his phone and asked a new question each time, so Dadu felt heard and remembered new details instead of just repeating.

qa.q: How did Sahil's view change over the week?
qa.a: Sahil went from bored and eye-rolling to curious enough to stay and ask his own question.

grounding: A young adult lets an elder tell the same story again and asks a new question each time, giving the elder a real hearing.

passage:
"Mehak, you asked how I got so patient with old people. Sit, let me tell you.
"When I was twenty, home from engineering college, my Ammachi would tell the same story every evening: how she came to Kottayam by boat as a bride, with one tin trunk. I knew it by heart. I used to finish her sentences to hurry her along.
"One evening I saw her face fall when I did it. She stopped mid-story and went to bed early.
"Next day, I tried something. When she started, I asked, 'Ammachi, what was in the trunk?' Her eyes lit up. Two saris, a Bible, and a jar of pickle from her mother. She'd never told anyone about the pickle.
"After that, I asked one new question each time. She didn't want to teach me anything, Mehak. She wanted to be listened to.
"When she died, Jomon, the one who finished her sentences, knew the most stories of all.

qa.q: What was in Ammachi's tin trunk?
qa.a: Two saris, a Bible, and a jar of pickle from her mother.

qa.q: What did Ammachi feel when young Jomon finished her sentences?
qa.a: Ammachi felt hurt and dismissed, her face falling so much that she stopped mid-story and went to bed early.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Jomon's story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Young Jomon asked what was in the trunk instead of hurrying her, and the new question made Ammachi feel heard and share a detail she had never told.

qa.q: How did the change affect Ammachi?
qa.a: Ammachi felt listened to and happy, her eyes lighting up as she shared new details.

grounding: An elder recalls learning, at twenty, to let a grandmother retell a story and ask a new question each time.

passage:
The power had been out for an hour in the Jaipur lane, and Kavitha sat with Lalit Uncle, her eighty-year-old neighbour, on his verandah with a candle and a hand fan. Her own phone was at five percent; her exam notes were waiting.
"Did I tell you about my tailoring shop near Johari Bazaar?" he asked.
He had, many times. The wedding sherwani, the rush before Diwali, the customer who never paid.
Kavitha glanced at her phone, then put it face down. "Tell me again. But this time, who was your first customer?"
Lalit Uncle blinked. "My first? A schoolteacher, Sharma ji. He wanted a kurta with pockets big enough for chalk." He laughed and laughed.
For forty minutes he talked. When the lights came back, he said, "You're a good listener, beti. My own sons only ask about my medicines."
Kavitha studied late that night, and didn't mind.

qa.q: How long had the power been out?
qa.a: The power had been out for an hour.

qa.q: What was Lalit Uncle feeling when he talked about Sharma ji?
qa.a: Lalit Uncle felt delighted and happy, laughing and laughing as he remembered his first customer.

qa.q: What choice did Kavitha make, and why did it help?
qa.a: She put her phone face down and asked a new question about the first customer, which made the old story fresh and made him feel heard.

qa.q: What would change if Kavitha had excused herself to study?
qa.a: Lalit Uncle would likely feel lonely and unheard, since he says even his sons only ask about his medicines.

grounding: A young adult lets an elder retell an old story and asks a new question, since the elder wants to be heard more than to instruct.

passage: Every Sunday after church, Francis climbed to the third floor of the Bandra building with a packet of Indu Aunty's favourite rusks. And every Sunday, between the first cup of tea and the second, she told the story again: her first day at the telephone exchange, the huge board of wires, the supervisor who shouted, the call she put through to the wrong city. Francis knew it by heart. His cousin had once asked, "You've heard it fifty times, why sit there?" But Francis had noticed that Indu Aunty's hands moved differently as she told it, quick and sure, as if plugging in wires. So each week he asked one new thing. Today: "What did you do with your first salary?" She stopped, then laughed. "I bought my mother a steel tiffin. She used it for twenty years." Her eyes were wet. "Nobody ever asked me that."

qa.q: What did Indu Aunty buy with her first salary?
qa.a: She bought her mother a steel tiffin.

qa.q: Why did Francis keep asking one new question each week?
qa.a: Francis felt fond of Indu Aunty and curious about her life; the way her hands came alive told him the story mattered to her.

qa.q: What small practice could someone borrow from Francis?
qa.a: When an elder repeats a story, stay and ask one fresh question, like the first-salary one, instead of saying "you told me already".

qa.q: What was it like for Indu Aunty to be asked about her first salary?
qa.a: She was surprised and moved, eyes wet, because nobody had ever asked, and it let her remember her mother and the tiffin.

grounding: Shows a young adult letting an elder tell the same story again and asking a fresh question each time, which makes the elder feel heard.
